name: Building AI-Powered Chatbots (No Programming Needed)
objectives: Given the questions your organization already receives, write a one-sentence job for a chatbot and list the ten questions it must answer, with no risky medical, legal or money questions on the list

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Planning and building the chatbot

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an AI chatbot can do, and picking its one job
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence job for a chatbot and list the questions it must answer.
This lesson builds toward: Given the questions your organization already receives, you will write a one-sentence job for a chatbot and list the ten questions it must answer, with no risky medical, legal or money questions on the list.
An AI chatbot is an AI assistant set up for one purpose. Instead of answering anything, it answers questions about your organization, using information you give it.
Good first jobs are narrow and repetitive: hours and location, prices, how to sign up, what to bring, return policies, volunteer shifts. Bad first jobs are risky ones: medical, legal or money advice, or anything that needs a person's judgment.
Start with the questions people already ask. Look at your emails, messages, phone calls and social media comments. The ten most common questions become the chatbot's job.
Step by step:
- Write down the ten questions people ask you most.
- Cross out any that need a person's judgment or are risky.
- Write the chatbot's job in one sentence: "This chatbot answers questions about [topic] for [who]."
Words to know:
- Chatbot: a program that answers questions in a chat window.
- Use case: the specific job a tool is used for.
Try it now: Pick a business, nonprofit or club (yours or a practice one). Write its ten most common questions and a one-sentence job for its chatbot.
You can now choose a safe, narrow job for a chatbot and list the questions it must answer.

check.q: What makes a good first job for a business chatbot?
options: Answering narrow, repeated questions like hours and sign-up
Answering any question in the world
check.why: Narrow, repetitive questions are low risk and save the most time.

check.q: Your barbershop gets many questions. Which one do you cross off the chatbot's list?
options: "Is this rash on my scalp serious?"
check.why: Health questions need a professional's judgment, so they are not a chatbot's job.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing the chatbot's instructions
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write clear instructions that set the chatbot's role, tone and limits.
This lesson builds toward: Using a no-code chatbot builder, you will write instructions that set the chatbot's role, audience, job, tone and limits, with all five parts and a line for what to do when it does not know.
No-code chatbot tools let you type instructions that the AI follows in every chat. Examples include custom GPTs in ChatGPT, Gems in Google Gemini and agents in Microsoft Copilot Studio. Feature names, menus and which plans include them change often, so check the tool's help page for the current steps.
Good instructions cover five things: who the chatbot is ("You are the help assistant for Sunrise Food Pantry"), who it talks to, what it answers, how it sounds (friendly, short, simple words), and what it must not do.
Write instructions as short, direct sentences. Tell it what to do when it does not know: "If the answer is not in the knowledge file, say you are not sure and give the phone number."
Step by step:
- Role: "You are the help assistant for [organization]."
- Audience: who will ask questions.
- Job: what topics it answers.
- Tone: friendly, short, simple words.
- Limits: what it must not do, and what to say when it does not know.
Words to know:
- Instructions: the standing directions a chatbot follows in every conversation; sometimes called a system prompt.
- Tone: how the writing sounds: formal, friendly, short.
Official sources:
- Google Gemini Help: Gems
Try it now: Write instructions for your chatbot with all five parts, in eight sentences or fewer.
You can now write chatbot instructions that set its role, audience, job, tone and limits.

check.q: Which part of the instructions is "friendly, short, simple words"?
check.why: Tone describes how the chatbot sounds.

check.q: Your instructions do not say what to do when the chatbot does not know. What do you add?
options: "Always give an answer, even a guess."
"If the answer is not in the knowledge file, say you are not sure and give the phone number."
check.why: Telling it to admit it is not sure and point to a person stops made-up answers.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Giving the chatbot your facts: the knowledge file
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a one-page knowledge file and connect it to a no-code chatbot.
This lesson builds toward: Given your organization's facts, you will create a one-page, dated knowledge file in question-and-answer form and add it to the chatbot, with no private information in it.
AI tools know a lot in general but nothing about your Tuesday hours. Most no-code chatbot builders let you upload a file, often under a section called Knowledge, that the chatbot uses to answer.
Make the file simple: a heading for each topic and short, plain facts. Use question-and-answer form for your top ten questions. Put the date at the top so you know when to update it.
Never put private information in the file: no customer names, phone numbers, passwords, donor details or bank information. Anything in the file could show up in an answer.
Step by step:
- Open a Google Doc or Word document.
- Add the date and the organization's name at the top.
- Write each top question with its answer underneath.
- Add basics: hours, address, contact, prices or services.
- Remove anything private, save it, and upload it in the chatbot builder's knowledge section.
Words to know:
- Knowledge file: a document you upload so the chatbot can answer from your facts.
- Upload: send a file from your device to a website or app.
Try it now: Write a one-page knowledge file for your chatbot with the date and your top ten questions answered. Then open a no-code chatbot builder you can use, paste your instructions, upload the file and save.
You can now build a safe knowledge file and connect it with instructions in a no-code chatbot builder.

check.q: Why put the date at the top of the knowledge file?
options: So you know when to update it
Because the AI needs it to start
check.why: The date shows how current the facts are and when to update them.

check.q: You are building a church's knowledge file. Which do you leave out?
options: How to join a small group
check.why: Private information like phone numbers could show up in an answer, so it never goes in the file.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Adding guardrails so the chatbot stays safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write guardrails that keep the chatbot on topic, honest and safe.
This lesson builds toward: For a chatbot the public will use, you will write guardrails that keep it on topic, honest and safe, including no private numbers, no professional advice, saying it is an AI and sending emergencies to 911.
Guardrails are rules that stop the chatbot from going where it should not. Add them to the instructions as clear "do not" and "always" lines.
Useful guardrails: stay on your topics and politely decline others; never ask for or store private details like card numbers or Social Security numbers; never give medical, legal or financial advice; tell people it is an AI, not a person; and send emergencies to 911 or the right hotline.
Being honest that it is AI builds trust. Start the chat with a short note: "Hi, I'm an AI assistant for Sunrise Food Pantry. I can answer questions about hours and what to bring."
Step by step:
- Add a line: stay on [your topics]; politely decline others.
- Add: never ask for card, bank, ID or Social Security numbers.
- Add: no medical, legal or financial advice; refer to a professional.
- Add: say you are an AI assistant.
- Add: for emergencies, tell people to call 911.
Words to know:
- Guardrail: a rule that keeps an AI tool on topic and safe.
- Decline: politely say no.
Try it now: Add at least five guardrails to your chatbot's instructions, plus a short greeting that says it is an AI assistant and what it can help with.
You can now write guardrails that keep a chatbot on topic, honest and safe.

check.q: What is the purpose of a guardrail in chatbot instructions?
options: To keep the chatbot on topic, honest and safe
check.why: Guardrails are "do not" and "always" rules that keep the chatbot where it should be.

check.q: A customer asks your shop's chatbot for their card number to finish an order. What should the guardrail make it do?
options: Ask for the full card number
Ask for only the last four digits
Never ask for card numbers, and point to the safe checkout or a person
Save the card number for next time
check.why: The chatbot must never ask for or store card, bank or ID numbers.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Testing the chatbot like a tough customer
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Test the chatbot with real and tricky questions, log the results and fix problems.
This lesson builds toward: Before anyone uses the chatbot, you will test it with at least ten real and tricky questions, log the results and fix failures, re-testing every failed question until it passes.
Never launch a chatbot you have not tested. Ask it at least ten questions: your top questions worded different ways, questions it should not answer, and tricky ones.
Tricky tests: ask about something not in the file (does it admit it does not know?), ask for advice it should decline, misspell words, and try to get it off topic ("Write me a poem"). Ask someone else to test it too; they will ask things you did not expect.
Keep a test log: the question, what it said, pass or fail, and the fix. Most fixes are small: add a missing fact to the knowledge file, or add a line to the instructions. Test again after each fix.
Step by step:
- Write ten test questions: common, reworded, off-topic and risky.
- Ask each one and copy the answer into a test log.
- Mark pass or fail.
- Fix failures by updating the knowledge file or instructions.
- Re-test the failed questions.
Words to know:
- Test log: a record of each test, the result and the fix.
- Edge case: an unusual question that can break a system.
Try it now: Run ten test questions on your chatbot, including at least three tricky ones. Record them in a test log, fix every failure and re-test.
You can now test a chatbot with common and tricky questions, keep a test log and fix what fails.

check.q: What goes in a chatbot test log?
options: Only the questions it got right
The question, the answer, pass or fail, and the fix
check.why: A test log records each question, the answer, pass or fail, and what you fixed.

check.q: During testing, the chatbot makes up a price that is not in your file. What do you do first?
options: Add the price to the knowledge file or a line telling it to admit it does not know, then re-test
Ignore it; customers will not ask
check.why: Most fixes are a missing fact or an instruction line, followed by a re-test.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Launching, sharing and keeping it up to date
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Share the chatbot with real users, collect feedback and set an update routine.
This lesson builds toward: When the chatbot is ready, you will share it with a few people, collect feedback and set an update routine, with a person always reachable for what it cannot handle.
Most builders let you share a chatbot with a link, and some let you add it to a website. Start small: share it with a few customers, members or volunteers first, and tell them it is new.
Ask for feedback: "Did it answer your question? What did it get wrong?" Read real conversations if your tool shows them, and look for questions it could not answer.
Set a routine. Every month, or any time hours, prices or policies change, update the knowledge file and its date. An outdated chatbot is worse than none. Keep a person reachable for anything the chatbot cannot handle.
Step by step:
- Share the chatbot link with three to five people.
- Ask them two feedback questions.
- Add missing answers to the knowledge file.
- Put a monthly update reminder on your calendar.
- Make sure people can always reach a person.
Words to know:
- Launch: make something available for people to use.
- Feedback: what users tell you about what worked and what did not.
Try it now: Final task: share your tested chatbot with at least one person. Write down their feedback, make one improvement, and set a monthly reminder to update the knowledge file.
You can now build, test, launch and maintain a no-code AI chatbot for a real organization.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear job No job sentence, or the job includes risky advice. A one-sentence job for a narrow, low-risk set of questions. The ten questions it covers come from real messages people sent. Instructions and guardrails Instructions are missing a role or any "do not" rules. Role, audience, job, tone and limits, plus guardrails for private numbers, advice, saying it is an AI and emergencies. Includes an opening note that tells people it is an AI and what it can help with. Knowledge file No file, or the file has private information. A dated, one-page file with the top questions and answers and no private information. Facts are grouped under clear headings and were checked by a second person. Test log Fewer than ten questions, or failures were not fixed. At least ten questions, including off-topic and risky ones, with fixes and re-tests. Someone else also tested it, and their questions are in the log. Feedback and upkeep Not shared, or no feedback written down. Shared with one person, feedback written down and a way to reach a person included. A monthly update reminder is set and one fix from the feedback is made. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why share a new chatbot with only a few people first?
options: Because links only work for five people
To find problems and get feedback before everyone uses it
So you never have to update it
check.why: Starting small lets you catch problems and gather feedback safely.

check.q: Your bakery changes its hours next week. What do you do with the chatbot?
options: Nothing; it will learn on its own
Update the knowledge file and its date
check.why: Update the file and its date whenever facts change; an outdated chatbot is worse than none.
